edits.defect: Asserted an ikhtilaf over rijz that none of the four fetched editions carries; the 'outward defilement' reading came only from the English translator's parenthetical.
edits.before: That inward half is where the commentators part ways over the word *rijz*. Some read it as outward defilement - the physical uncleanness the water washed off. Al-Muyassar reads it as the inward disturbance itself: the whispering, the passing thoughts that press on a heart under pressure. The translation above renders it "filth," and the word is wide enough to carry both. The verse does not force a choice; one rainfall lifts both kinds of impurity.
edits.after: That inward half rests on the word *rijz*, and the commentators are notably of one mind about it. Al-Muyassar reads it as the inward disturbance itself: the whispering, the passing thoughts that press on a heart under pressure. Al-Jalalayn glosses it *waswasatuhu*, his whispering. Ibn Kathir has "his whispers and evil thoughts," and names that as the inner purification. And the report al-Tabari carries from Mujahid says the same in one word: *waswasatuhu*. The English translation above renders *rijz* as "filth," which sounds outward, but the outward washing is already named in the clause just before it - *li-yutahhirakum bihi*. One rainfall lifts both kinds of impurity, and the commentators put *rijz* on the inner side of the pair.
edits.evidence: All four editions gloss rijz inwardly. al-Muyassar 8:11: 'ويزيل عنكم في الباطن وساوس الشيطان وخواطره'. al-Jalalayn 8:11: '﴿ويُذْهِب عَنْكُمْ رِجْز الشَّيْطان﴾ وسْوَسَته إلَيْكُمْ'. Ibn Kathir 8:11 (English): '(and to remove from you the Rijz of Shaytan,) such as his whispers and evil thoughts, this involves inner purification'. al-Tabari 8:11 transmits Mujahid twice: '﴿رجز الشيطان﴾، قال: وسوسته' and '"رجز الشيطان"، وسوسته'; the editor's own footnote notes al-Tabari gave no separate gloss of his own ('أغفل أبو جعفر هنا إفراد تفسير "يذهب عنكم رجز الشيطان"'), which is why the new text attributes only the Mujahid report to him rather than a judgment of his own. Nothing in the four supports an 'outward defilement' reading of rijz; the only outward element is the separate clause li-yutahhirakum (Ibn Kathir: 'to clean you thereby ... this involves cleansing what is on the outside').
